title: Are Japanese temples on Mt Koya cashing in on the foreign tourism boom?
description: With more than 100 million yen in underreported income, questions are being raised over the morals of profiting from overseas tourists. A lot of businesses and organisations in Japan are seeking to make the most of the current boom in tourism by finding new ways to promote themselves and appeal to the foreign tourist market. […]
content:
With more than 100 million yen in underreported income, questions are being raised over the morals of profiting from overseas tourists.

A lot of businesses and organisations in Japan are seeking to make the most of the current boom in tourism by finding new ways to promote themselves and appeal to the foreign tourist market.

However, when that organisation is tied up with religion, it can blur the lines between what’s morally right and wrong, which is the situation that Japan’s world-famous religious site Mt Koya has now found itself in.

Located in the mountains of Wakayama Prefecture, Mt Koya has long been a revered religious site for pilgrims, and is so special it’s part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The site draws tourists from around the world, with many wanting to fully immerse themselves in the otherworldly spirit of the holy mountain by staying in temple accommodation, known as shukubo.

▼ Mt Koya, or “Koyasan” as it’s known in Japanese.

Following a recent tax investigation, it was found that religious corporations operating shukubo on Mt Koya had underreported more than 100 million yen (US$650,000) in income collectively, with around 90 million yen attributed to one temple, Sojiin. In this case, the family of the chief priest was found to have used income from the temple lodging for personal expenses over a three-year period. The tax authorities treated this as undeclared remuneration, and the religious corporation was hit with around 40 million yen in additional taxes and penalties.

The issue came to light on 10 September, when reports emerged that the Osaka Regional Taxation Bureau had investigated more than 10 religious corporations operating shukubo on Mt Koya, with more than half of those investigated found to have failed to properly declare income. The news was widely reported in Japan, putting the spotlight on how religious organisations are making money from the current tourism boom.

In terms of taxes, income from religious activities such as donations and offerings is generally exempt from taxation, while income earned through revenue-generating businesses such as accommodation is taxable. So although staying at a temple may be part of a spiritual or cultural experience, if that temple is operating accommodation as a business, the income it earns from those stays is subject to tax.

▼ Mt Koya is dotted with moss-covered religious sites and graves.

There’s certainly plenty of money being made from tourist stays. Mt Koya has 117 temples, 51 of which operate shukubo, and in 2025 around 117,500 foreign guests stayed overnight on the mountain, a 10-percent increase from the previous year. Shukubo, which traditionally provided accommodation for monks and pilgrims, have become increasingly popular with tourists from overseas, offering experiences such as Buddhist vegetarian meals, morning services, meditation and sutra copying.

As the number of foreign visitors has increased, so too has the price of temple stays, with some rooms on Mt Koya now costing more than 150,000 yen for two adults per night. According to one visitor, the same temple charging those prices now was only charging roughly 20,000 to 30,000 yen per person just four years ago.

The Koyasan Shukubo Association says that around 40 years ago, a one-night stay with two meals cost about 7,000 yen. Since the pandemic, government subsidies helped some lodgings upgrade their facilities, contributing to what the association describes as a move towards more luxurious accommodation. Today, some shukubo can offer rooms and facilities that look more like those of a luxury ryokan than the humble temple lodgings used by visitors in the past.

▼ Many of the temples on Mt Koya have histories that stretch back hundreds of years.

From the standpoint of the temples, running accommodation requires staff, food, maintenance and other expenses, and they are operating in a tourism market where visitors are increasingly willing to pay for a more comfortable and exclusive experience. At the same time, these are still religious sites, and the more they resemble luxury hotels and charge luxury prices, the more questions are raised about where the line should be drawn between providing a sustainable service and commercialising a sacred space.

However, the rising prices have not gone over well with a lot of tourists, with Japanese visitors also asking the question: “Are temples supposed to be profit-seeking?”

It’s a tough balance to strike between providing a religious service and earning money to keep old traditions alive. But with the weak yen making experiences that are expensive by Japanese standards seem incredibly cheap to overseas tourists, price increases in the tourist sector are now becoming increasingly common.

Whether these increases are justified or not is up for debate, but when one of the country’s most famous temple communities is involved, there needs to be extra transparency in income reporting and careful thought given to how much is too much when charging for overnight stays.

Sources: Yomiuri Shimbun, Sankei via Yahoo! Japan News

title: Visiting Kagawa’s popular cooking class where you make noodles with your feet
description: Rock out as you dance your way to handmade sanuki udon. Having a meal out is a great experience now and again, but cooking for yourself not only allows you to customize your meal to your liking, it also provides you with a warming sense of accomplishment. However, having a professional by your side to […]
content:
Rock out as you dance your way to handmade sanuki udon.

Having a meal out is a great experience now and again, but cooking for yourself not only allows you to customize your meal to your liking, it also provides you with a warming sense of accomplishment. However, having a professional by your side to gently guide you along the steps to making a famous local food is on a level of its own—particularly when it involves dancing on top of your dough.

▼ Don’t worry, it doesn’t smell like feet.

Kagawa, located on Shikoku, the smallest of Japan’s four main islands, is not one of the nation’s main tourist hubs, and even our Japanese-language reporter Kouhey has only been there a scant two times in the past. It is a well-known home to sanuki udon noodles, which are thick, chewy, and have been proven to calm crying babies, and yet Kouhey has hardly ever eaten the food in this land of noodles, so for his most recent trip there, he sought to remedy this travesty.

The town of Kotohira is a popular tourist destination within Kagawa, famous for Kotohira Shrine (affectionately known as Kompirasan) and its climb with over 700 steps. At the foot of the shrine is Nakano Udon School, a company that is over a century old and has been offering sanuki udon experiences for tourists for over 40 years. It also featured in the post credits scene of Episode 452 of Detective Conan, “The Phantom of Konpira.” Surely such a well-established company would be able to show Kouhey the way to the most delicious noodles.

Of course, being a person with strong impulsive tendencies, Kouhey hadn’t actually planned on delving into the kitchen himself, but he figured “why not?” and waltzed up to the door where the class schedule for the day was posted. There were three columns for the three different classrooms in Building A, Building B, and the West Building. On the day that he was there, only the column for Building B had time plates hung up for 9:30 a.m. and 1:00 p.m., indicating available classes on that day.

Going up to the reception to ask, Kouhey was told the class would take about 50 minutes, and he was in luck as there happened to still be space available to participate. The staff also mentioned that on some days the classes get completely booked, so if you want to make sure you get to experience it, booking in advance on the website is the way to go.

If you participate alone and take the noodles home, like Kouhey, it costs 1,980 yen (US$13), but if you eat them on-site, it’s 2,530 yen. For groups of up to 14 people, it’s 1,760 yen per person, and for 15 or more, it’s 1,650 yen, so be sure to drag all of your friends along for an experience you’re unlikely to forget. Note that for groups, the price doesn’t change whether you take them home or eat them on the spot, so it’s pretty reasonable.

After registering, Kouhey was given the option of what souvenir to take home: a Secret Recipe Scroll that doubles as a rolling pin, or two servings of udon. Without much hesitation, he opted for the scroll.

▼ We’d show you the inside, but… it’s a secret.

As he turned around to wait for the time of the class to start, Kouhey spotted the Nakano Udon School Graduate Signatures from celebrities hanging on the wall, remarking how school-like it felt to have them be called “graduates”.

When he finally entered the venue, Kouhey came to find that the class would be held in a school classroom-esque setting.

Looking around, there were over 20 people, including families with children, with almost all of the seats filled. A male instructor with a dark blue hand towel wrapped around his head stood in front holding a microphone when…

♪~Ding Dong Dang Dong~♪

…Japan’s iconic school chime rang out, and the class began.

First up, Kouhey was handed a lump of dough shaped like a rectangle with rounded corners, which he needed to roll out.

Roll it out, wind it around the rolling pin, and roll it out again.

After that, Kouhey just had to cut it with a knife.

Looking at his completed work closer, Kouhey spotted thick and thin cuts of different sizes, but overall he was pretty pleased with how his first-ever noodles came out.

These noodles could either be boiled and eaten in the cafeteria on the floor below after the class ended, or taken home to cook, which was what Kouhey had chosen to do.

Now, it was time for the main event: making the dough from scratch. First was the process of mixing flour with salted water. The flour goes into the kneading bowl (called a “konebachi”) and the salted water is added from the red cup.

Stirring with fingers held upright, the flour gradually turns into a crumbly texture.

Put this into a plastic bag and flatten it out. Next up was “foot-kneading”.

Place the dough inside a bag on top of a tatami mat, and step on it with just your socks on. While a novel experience, it’s made countless times more fun thanks to the upbeat background music played in the classroom for this part of the lesson, causing you to dance on top of your dough.

It’s hard to tell only by looking at Kouhey’s feet, but dough was being stomped on everywhere around him while the other students also danced along to exciting tracks, bringing out the inner kids in all of the adults. Back in 2016, when I visited the school myself, I rocked out to Gangnam Style and PPAP, with my fellow “classmates” playing the tambourines—ten out of ten, the most fun cooking experience I’ve had to date.

Fold the flattened dough into layers, form it into a rough baumkuchen/roll cake shape, where it will then enter the aging process, which can vary depending on the season. This brings the class to a close.

Under the graduation commemoration sign at the back of the classroom, families and groups of friends lined up to take their photos.

After returning home, Kouhey finally had a chance to compare and eat the udon he had bought at the Nakano Udon School gift shop against the noodles he had rolled and cut himself.

▼ Kouhey’s noodles are on the right.

The moment Kouhey boiled them and arranged them on a plate, they were already clearly different. The noodles from the gift shop had a round cross-section and were neatly uniform in thickness. On the other hand, his noodles were flat, wide, and uneven in thickness.

He had lost in terms of appearance, but it being his first time trying to cut noodles, he had kind of been expecting it.

As for the taste, the gift shop noodles were naturally chewy and delicious.

In contrast, Kouhey’s noodles were missing that ideal firm-on-the-outside, chewy-on-the-inside texture, perhaps because he boiled them too long.

Even so, the emotional impact of eating his own noodles was exceptional. Kouhey may eat oodles of noodles in the future, but he has a newfound respect for the time and effort used to make such delicious food from nothing more than flour, salt, and water, all thanks to this single class he attended. If ever you are in the area, making your own noodles is an experience that you shouldn’t pass on by.

Nakano Udon Gakko Kotohira-ko / 中野うどん学校 琴平校
Address: Kagawa-ken, Nakatada-gun, Kotohira-cho 796

title: Pokémon Adidas crossover sneaker line releases in Japan, gives your feet Pikachu hugs [Pics]
description: Collaboration gets off to an early start in Pokémon’s home country. There’s a lot of walking in Pokémon. The young Trainers who serve as the protagonists of the video games and anime are generally too young to drive, and besides, catching ‘em all involves venturing far afield in order to find the rarest Pocket Monster […]
content:
Collaboration gets off to an early start in Pokémon’s home country.

There’s a lot of walking in Pokémon. The young Trainers who serve as the protagonists of the video games and anime are generally too young to drive, and besides, catching ‘em all involves venturing far afield in order to find the rarest Pocket Monster breeds.

So if you’ve got some real-world walking of your own to do, Adidas wants to let you do it in Pokémon sneakers.

The Pokémon 30th Anniversary Adidas Originals line is now on sale in Japan, with the crossover combining some of the most iconic Pokémon with some of Adidas most popular footwear models. Pikachu, naturally, shows up multiple times, first in the Superstar II mid-tops above, with a textured Pikachu hugging your ankles. Meanwhile, the low-top Pikachu Superstar II focuses on the face of the franchise’s ears, while also recreating his fluffy fur on the shoes’ outside.

Two different smile-inducing smiling Pikachus can be found around back, but if you want even more of them walking with you, these will do the trick.

The colors of the Charmander Superstar II will immediately evoke happy memories of time spent with the Gen-I starter…

…and the flames on the side will remind even newer fans know that this is a Fire-type.

Speaking of Charmander, Adidas’ Pokémon collection marks a rare occasion for Charmeleon, Charmander’s first evolution (i.e. his form before evolving into Charizard) to enjoy some time in the spotlight with its own Superstar II version.

Ghost-type fashion comes in the form of a menacing Gengar Adistar XLG 2.0…

…and Haunter Adistar Control 5, which has a more subtle nod to its inspiration in the shape of the shoe’s tongue.

Rayquaza shows up twice, befitting its importance as a Legendary Pokémon, with both Megaride and ZX 500 RS versions…

…or, if you want to show off a real old-school Legendary Pokémon, there’s the Mewtwo Samba OG

Adidas tends to put aesthetics before affordability in its limited-edition models, and the shoes shown above range in price from 16,500 to 33,000 yen (approximately US$105-US$210). They’re available as of September 15 in Japan through the Adidas Japan online shop and Rakuten (here and here), and are scheduled to start making their way to overseas retailers starting September 22.

title: Starbucks and clothing brand Beams team up for launch of second collaborative core collection
description: You can wear your love for coffee on your sleeve in this new series of Starbucks Stand by Beams clothing and lifestyle goods–literally, in one case. It’s been a year since Starbucks Japan teamed up with Japanese clothing brand Beams for a joint “Starbucks Stand by Beams” collaboration. Following the success of that first series […]
content:
You can wear your love for coffee on your sleeve in this new series of Starbucks Stand by Beams clothing and lifestyle goods–literally, in one case.

It’s been a year since Starbucks Japan teamed up with Japanese clothing brand Beams for a joint “Starbucks Stand by Beams” collaboration. Following the success of that first series of items that blended fashion and coffee culture, the giants are now gearing up to release a second series in the core collection.

▼ Starbucks Stand by Beams is not even the first time that the two major brands have teamed up for apparel.

The new line will debut on September 18 with 14 types of items, with one each sold exclusively at the Starbucks online shop and Beams stores respectively. All clothing items are unisex and come in sizes extra-small through extra-large, though the Starbucks online shop carries sizes small through extra-large only.

● Logo ringer t-shirts (9,350 yen [US$61])

This timeless design comes in either beige or blue colors with darker accents along the neckline and sleeve hemlines. It’s a made of a rayon blend of heathered fabric.

● Logo zipper hoodies (19,800 yen)

A USA cotton fleece lining lends the ultimate comfort to these brown, green, oatmeal-colored full-zip hoodies.

 

● Logo sweatpants (16,500 yen)

With the same colors to match the above hoodies, these wide sweatpants feature a heavyweight USA cotton fleece lining. They also include a length adjuster and a zippered back pocket.

● Oxford shirt (15,400 yen, exclusive to the Starbucks online shop)

A cute tumbler embroidery graces the front left pocket of this wide-fit Oxford shirt made of heavyweight cotton.

   

● Flap chino pants (19,800 yen, exclusive to Beams stores)

Dress up or dress down in these classically comfortable olive, beige, or brown chino pants that come with flap pockets and adjustable hems.

● Black denim jacket (41,800 yen)

Made with denim from Japan’s leading denim-producing area, Okayama, the jacket’s initial color is faded then subsequently washed using discarded coffee bean husks for a dark, natural coffee hue (there’s no word yet on whether it’s coffee-scented as well).

● Natural color logo PVC pouch (3,960 yen)

This multiuse pouch features different logos on each side, including the familiar Starbucks siren. Its PVC material is water and stain-resistant.

● Clear color logo PVC pouch (3,300 yen)

This one is another multiuse pouch but this time transparent for you to be able to see what’s stored inside.

● Craft paper cool bag (7,150 yen)

Made from Tyvek material, this lunch bag resembles the paper bags given with Starbucks food orders. Built-in aluminum-coated insulation keeps the food inside cool and mesh pockets help you keep things separated.

● Synthetic leather drawstring bag (12,100 yen)

On the slightly more stylish end, this black drawstring bag has two-way functionality with its removable shoulder strap.

● Logo PVC shoulder tote bag (8,800 yen)

Meanwhile, this small tote is perfect for everyday use and is equipped with an interior pocket and carabiner for extra security.

● Coffee cherry bandana (2,970 yen)

These brown and navy-colored bandanas can serve a variety of practical or aesthetic purposes with their intricate design of coffee berries (commonly called “coffee cherries”), leaves, and flowers in a lacelike pattern.

● Drink-ID socks (3,300 yen)

White-and-black socks with the drink customization chart found on the back of Starbucks cups are perfect for that person who customizes every part of their drink. They come in two sizes–small (23-25 centimeters [9-9.8 inches]) and medium (25-27 centimeters).

● To-go bottles (5,800 yen)

The last new item in the core collection is a beige or navy stainless steel bottle designed to capture the look of Starbucks’ paper cups. It has double-layered vacuum insulation, a locking lid, and stores 473 milliliters (16 fluid ounces) of liquid.

 

The Starbucks Stand by Beams collection will be available starting September 18 appear at the Beams Life store in Yokohama, Beams Japan store in Tokyo’s Shinjuku district, and the new Beams Umeda tore in Osaka, as well as at a pop-up store that runs until September 27 at Nagoya Station.

We look forward to seeing what other kinds of creative collaborations Beams takes on next!

title: Ghibli/Kyoto crossover artwork decorates goshuin papers for Zen and Ghibli art exhibition [Pics]
description: Kyoto museum’s ”Ghibli for grown-ups” event collaborates with three Kyoto Zen temples. Temple architecture and anime artwork are both undeniable expressions of Japanese aesthetic sensibilities. Many would say that some of the finest examples of the former can be found in Kyoto, and the latter within the films of Studio Ghibli, and this fall JR […]
content:
Kyoto museum’s ”Ghibli for grown-ups” event collaborates with three Kyoto Zen temples.

Temple architecture and anime artwork are both undeniable expressions of Japanese aesthetic sensibilities. Many would say that some of the finest examples of the former can be found in Kyoto, and the latter within the films of Studio Ghibli, and this fall JR Central is offering something special for fans who enjoy both.

The Kyoto City Kyocera Museum of Art is getting ready to open its Zen and Ghibli exhibition in October. This first-of-its-kind event is “an immersive exhibition exploring Zen through the works of Studio Ghibli,” drawing from a book of the same title written by veteran Ghibli producer Toshio Suzuki. The museum says that “Ghibli films often embody a worldview that does not divide good and evil, leaves space instead of rushing to answers, and embraces the attitude of ‘accepting without fully understanding.’ This resonates deeply with the Zen principles of ‘not dividing,’ ‘not judging,’ and ‘seeing things as they are,’” and the exhibit is structured around The Boy and the Heron, arguably Ghibli’s most open-to-interpretation anime ever, in particular.

▼　The poster for Zen and Ghibli, which the museum is also promoting as “Ghibli-for grown-ups,” features a line of The Boy and the Heron’ s floating warara creatures.

At-the-door admission is 1,900 yen (US$12), but getting your ticket in advance via JR Central’s EX ticketing service will save you 300 yen if you book by October 2, and it’ll still save you 100 yen after that date. More importantly, though, booking through EX will get you some beautiful Ghibli/Kyoto collaborative artwork in the form of goshuin papers.

Goshuin are stamped certificates provided at temples in Japan, certifying the bearer’s visit and said to bestow blessings upon them. They also look really cool, and many travelers enjoy them as a culturally artistic way of commemorating that part of their journey. In the most basic arrangement, the goshuin is transferred onto plain white paper, but the JR Central-reserved Zen and Ghibli ticket includes Ghibli-themed goshuin papers to be used at three famous Kyoto temples. Pictured above is the paper to be used at Shokokuji Temple, with Totoro flying above the temple’s main hall, and there are also papers for Nanzenji and Myoshinji Temples.

▼ The Nanzenji paper features Porco Rosso protagonist Porco.

▼ The Myoshinji paper has who appears to be Howl’s Moving Castle’s Howl in his avian form, but with a bit of a simian touch.

▼ Maybe it’s meant as a nod to “Withered Trees and Monkeys,” a famous work by 16th/17th-century painter Hasegawa Tohaku which has been in Myoshinji’s collection of artwork.

The goshuin papers start off with their left halves blank, as the stamps are to be added upon visiting the respective temples. Alternatively, if you’re a hybrid Ghilbi/goshuin enthusiast who wants something more substantial to be stamped, JR Central is also offering a package with a Zen and Ghibli admission ticket and a goshuin book, with multiple blank pages inside, a front cover illustrated with the adorable warawara, and Princess Mononoke’s San on the back.

Note that while admission to the Zen and Ghibli exhibit is included in the JR Central packages, admission to the three associated temples is separate, as are the fees for the goshuin stamp to be applied.

The packages can be reserved now through the EX website here, with the museum ticket/goshuin papers set 1,600 yen and the ticket/goshuin book bundle 3,300 yen until October 2, and the prices for both going up by 200 yen after that. Zen and Ghibli is scheduled to run from October 3 to December 6, but the goshuin papers/book can be used after the exhibition closes as well.

content:
A beniharuka shake rolls into Sukiya as sweet potato season gets underway.

Japan never met a seasonal sweets flavor it couldn’t find space in its heart for, and with sweet potato season here, it’s an especially sweet time of year. The flavor of sweet potatoes is so loved in Japan that there’s even a whole sub-category of sweet potato dessert drinks that arrives every autumn, such as Starbucks Japan’s sweet potato Frappuccino.

But cafes and coffeehouses don’t have a monopoly on drinkable sweet potato treats, and one of the best we’ve had so far this year is at none other than one of Japan’s biggest beef bowl chains.

Along with Yoshinoya and Matsuya, Sukiya is one of Japan’s big three gyudon (beef bowl) restaurants, and their take on the dish has a subtle hint of refreshing citrus to the broth the meat is simmered in.

But Sukiya is ready to satisfy not just carnivorous cravings, as they’ve also got a selection of desserts that they collectively call the “Suki Cafe” line, which includes their Suki Shakes, and as of September 8 they’re serving up sweet potato shakes!

If you’re ordering in Japanese, the flavor is called yakiimo, which translates literally as “roasted potato” but is always used to refer specifically to roasted sweet potatoes. Suki Shakes are generally a vanilla base with another flavor mixed in for an enticing marbled appearance, and in this case the special guest is a sweet potato sauce made with beniharuka grown in Ibaraki Prefecture. Beniharuka are Japan’s sweetest variety of sweet potato, so we had high expectations as we took a sip.

The first thing to register on our taste buds was the milky sweetness of the vanilla portion, which is so creamy that it reminded us of soft-serve ice cream. After that came the sweet potato sauce, which not only tasted delicious but had a stickiness to it, evoking thoughts of the caramelized sugar that seeps out of sweet potatoes during roasting. It was a fantastic combination, and with the crushed pieces of imo kenpi (crisp candied sweet potato chips) sprinkled across the top, you also get some stimulating crunchiness.

Our taste tester Yayoi Saginomiya was so impressed that she’s ready to call this a dark horse contender for the best sweet potato drink you can find this season. In addition to being a far, far more delicious dessert than most people would expect of a beef bowl restaurant, it’s a very affordable one too, costing just 210 yen (US$1.30) for a small size, 260 for a medium, and 350 for a large, so stomach capacity, not budget concerns, is going to be the only limiting factor as to how many of these we can drink during the limited time they’ll be on sale.

title: Making the latest social media snack sensation in Japan, Dot Butter
description: High in both cuteness and calories. The advent of the Internet enabled sharing of strange ways to eat food to a degree never before seen in human history. Whether it’s putting pudding in ramen, eating ramen in a bathtub, or adding sake to ramen, there’s no shortage of ideas that make you wonder both why […]
content:
High in both cuteness and calories.

The advent of the Internet enabled sharing of strange ways to eat food to a degree never before seen in human history. Whether it’s putting pudding in ramen, eating ramen in a bathtub, or adding sake to ramen, there’s no shortage of ideas that make you wonder both why they thought of such a thing and why you never thought of such a thing.

The latest such creation is going by the name of “Dot Butter” on social media. It’s both incredibly simple and unheard of at the same time, simply consisting of a piece of butter with sprinkles. I personally have never felt the urge to eat a spoonful of butter, and I’m not sure sprinkles would sweeten the deal all that much, but one look was enough to give our writer Mai Tsubomi the urge to try some Dot Butter for herself.

She headed to her local supermarket and came home with a pack of sprinkles and some butter. Mai figured the type of butter sold in pre-cut and individually wrapped squares would work well for this particular snack.

Making Dot Butter is extremely simple. Just coat the piece of butter in sprinkles and eat. However, after plopping in her pre-cut butter, Mai noticed a problem.

The piece of butter was a little too small compared to the size of the sprinkles. Because of this, the sprinkles wouldn’t stick everywhere on the butter, leaving bare patches here and there. It turned out that this recipe wasn’t quite as easy as it seems.

It didn’t quite have the visual impact she was hoping for and still felt like she was about to bite into a chunk of butter. Our writer initially panicked, thinking she somehow managed to screw up one of the easiest recipes around. However, once she tasted it, she was pleasantly surprised. The saltiness of the butter mingled well with the sweetness of the sprinkles.

Luckily, Mai’s first experience with Dot Butter was a good one, but she still felt like it could have been better. So she went to the kitchen, got a stick of regular butter, and cut off a piece large enough to fully accept the sprinkles while also keeping her own health in mind as one should when eating pure butter.

It looked much better and tasted just as good at first, but a few more bites in and she began to notice an oily film form in her mouth. It became too much to bear, and she decided to spread the remainder on some toast instead. Clearly, balance was the key in creating Dot Butter that’s both good-looking and pleasant to eat.

With this new taste sensation under her belt, Mai started to wonder what if more commonly edible dairy squares were used in the place of butter. So she also prepared the ingredients to make Dot Cream Cheese and Dot Mozzarella.

Fortunately for our writer, both came out surprisingly good. In fact, she’d say they were both better than Dot Butter. The Dot Cream Cheese was the better of the two, with a delicious tang and the feeling of eating some cheesecake. Dot Mozzarella, on the other hand, had the same delectable balance of sweet and salty that the butter had, but without the greasy mouthfeel.

She still felt Dot Butter itself is a really nice treat when done in moderation and had a certain forbidden charm that the other squares were somewhat lacking in. One thing to point out is that most sprinkles in Japan are made from chocolate, and results may vary when using sugar-based sprinkles, though I can’t imagine how. So go ahead and add a little color to your life from time to time.

title: 7-Eleven Japan releases a Kebab Sandwich… but does it really taste like a street-stall kebab?
description: We find out if a convenience store kebab can compete with the real thing. In recent years, kebab stores have become common around Tokyo, with huge barrels of meat no longer being a strange curiosity but a serious craving. 7-Eleven is now catching on to this trend by serving up its own version of a […]
content:
We find out if a convenience store kebab can compete with the real thing.

In recent years, kebab stores have become common around Tokyo, with huge barrels of meat no longer being a strange curiosity but a serious craving. 7-Eleven is now catching on to this trend by serving up its own version of a kebab, in the form of a Chicken Kebab Sandwich.

This was something we were surprised to see when we visited a branch the other day, and our curiosity immediately got the better of us. Keen to find out just how kebab-like the sandwich would be, especially with sliced white bread instead of pita holding it together, we plucked one off the shelf and took it home for a taste test.

The first thing we noticed upon opening it, was the filling, which seemed to have everything you’d want in a kebab sandwich – chicken, tomato, cabbage and lettuce. Though it was generous, it wasn’t overflowing to the point of falling out everywhere, which is what usually happens when we hold a kebab.

The fact that we could hold it in one hand and easily bite into it made this a very convenient kebab, which is what you’d ideally want from a convenience store, but the big question was… how would it taste?

Taking a bite, our eyes widened with glee as we were amazed by just how authentic the fillings were! For us, the sauce is always the key to a good kebab, and that distinctive, spicy sauce with a slightly herbal accent had been properly recreated.

The sauce helped to lift the ingredients and bring them together to deliver an authentic kebab flavour. One thing that really surprised us, though, was the kick, as the sauce was quite spicy, despite only measuring one out of three chilli peppers on the rating scale. It was a hot, tingling, slightly fiery spiciness so if you don’t like spicy food, you might want to tread with caution here.

As lovers of spicy food, this was no problem for us, though, and in fact, it was a very welcome surprise. The heat only added to our overall appreciation for the sandwich, but before polishing it off, there was one more thing we had to test: the cross section. Convenience stores are known for committing what’s become known as “cross-section fraud”, where the sandwich looks full at the cross section but lacks ingredients towards the back of the slice.

Peeling the sandwich apart, we were happy to find there was no cross-section fraud here, as the sandwich was nicely filled to all three sides. This earned it another tick in our books, making it an all-star in terms of looks, ease-of-eating, portion size and flavour. There was only one point of contention, as it could be argued that, at 429 yen (US$2.79), it’s not that cheap, so you might be better off buying an actual kebab from a kebab shop.

However, there’s something to be said about the convenience of being able to pick up a tasty kebab at 7-Eleven. Not only is it a treat to know you can satisfy a craving for a kebab at any hour of the day or night, it’s especially nice for people outside of big cities, where kebabs aren’t as readily available.

Much like the taco burrito that came before it, 7-Eleven’s kebab sandwich is a great way to introduce more people to flavours from around the world, and remind us all that Japan knows how to do a great sandwich, even when it’s not filled with fruit and chocolate chips.

title: The confusing enjoyment of our day-trip bus tour from downtown Tokyo to Yamanashi [Photos]
description: This bus tour wasn’t exactly what we’d expected, but it turned out to be something we wanted. “Shinjuku-Departure Sunflowers & Peach-picking & All-You-Can-Pack Kikyo Shingen Mochi & Heidi Village.” With a name that thorough, our Japanese-language reporter Asami Oshima figured she knew exactly what was going to be in store for her on this bus […]
content:
This bus tour wasn’t exactly what we’d expected, but it turned out to be something we wanted.

“Shinjuku-Departure Sunflowers & Peach-picking & All-You-Can-Pack Kikyo Shingen Mochi & Heidi Village.”

With a name that thorough, our Japanese-language reporter Asami Oshima figured she knew exactly what was going to be in store for her on this bus tour that departs from the Shinjuku neighborhood in downtown Tokyo and takes travelers on a day-trip to Yamanashi Prefecture. And yet, there still turned out to be some surprises waiting for her.

Asami’s trip started from the Tocho Large Bus Parking Lot, located near the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (Tocho), to the west of Shinjuku Station. There were about 50 people taking part in the tour this day, and though the scheduled departure time was 7:40 a.m., the group was punctual enough that everyone was present and checked in early, so they got moving at 7:35.

▼ The sticker from tour operator Travel Road’s Buttobi Tours (“Hopping Tours”), identifying Asami as a member of the day’s group.

It’s about a 90-minute drive from Tokyo to the peach farm that was the first stop on the itinerary. After an hour on the road, they stopped at the Dangozaka Service Area highway rest stop in Uenohara, Yamanashi, so that anyone who needed to could use the bathroom or stretch their legs.

Like most rest stops of at least average size in Japan, the Dangozaka Service Area has a lot of tempting food options. Walking around, Asami was strongly tempted by the skewered mochi dumplings and wagyu on offer, but she resisted the urge to start stuffing her face, since she knew there was going to be plenty of food to come later in the day.

After the 20-minutes break, the bus rolled out again, and at 9:35, they arrived at Watanabe Farm in the town of Fuefuki.

▼ From Tokyo to Watanabe Farm

This is where the group was supposed to pick peaches, which Yamanashi is famous for, and also be able to eat as many as they wanted within a set amount of time. After getting off the bus, Asami assumed that they were going to be led into the orchard, but instead the group was guided to an array of outdoor tables that already had crates of peaches, and plums too, on them.

It turned out that the fruit for the all-you-can-eat session had already been picked ahead of time for the group, so instead of grabbing them off the trees, you selected them from the crates, then peeled and sliced them for yourself.

This isn’t the way fruit-picking activities are usually done in Japan, but everything did taste good, and no time spent picking meant more time for eating. It did feel a little surreal, though, to be part of such a large group of people single-mindedly and diligently peeling and munching on fruit for 30 minutes.

Once the half-hour was up, though, there was time for some actual fruit picking. Everyone got back on the bus and rode five minutes to the orchard, where they were allowed to pick one peach each.

Their next stop was also located in Fuefuki, the Kikyo Shingen Mochi Theme Park.

Shingen Mochi is Yamanashi’s representative confectionary, a sort of jiggly mochi dusted with a large amount of kinako (roasted soybean powder) and drizzled with a sweet, sticky brown sugar sauce.

▼ The standard Shingen Mochi comes in a plastic container, but there’s also a special version with an edible wafer shell.

Here, again, the terminology is kind of confusing, since the Kikyo Shingen Mochi Theme Park isn’t what most people would call a theme park. Instead, it’s a Shingen Mochi factory that offers tours that show how the sweets are made.

Guests can also try their hand at packing Shingen Mochi into a bag, and can keep as many as they can fit in as long as the top can still be tied shut.

Everyone starts off with eight Shingen Mochi packs to put in their bag, and some truly tactilely talented visitors have been able to stuff 22 inside, as shown in the example placard.

However, while ordinarily purchased Shingen Mochi will keep for a little longer, the staff informed the tour participants that the sweets they could pack into their bags had a best-by date of the following day. Hearing this, Asami felt a little bummed that she wouldn’t be able to build up a war chest of desserts to snack on at her leisure over the coming week.

And yet, as she followed the advice provided by their guide and began stretching the bag with her hands to get it to loosen up and hold more mochi, she felt herself getting a little giddy at the prospect of seeing how many she could claim.

In the end, she managed to fit 10 inside, plenty for her to enjoy for herself and still have enough to pass off to friends or coworkers the next day as souvenirs.

After leaving the mochi factory, it was about a half-hour ride to Heidi Village.

This actually is sort of like a theme park, though a quaint, countryside one with shops and restaurants instead of parades and roller coasters. The Heidi novel was adapted into a year-long anime TV series in 1974, with soon-to-be-famous industry giants like Studio Ghibli co-founders Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata, plus Mobile Suit Gundam creator Yoshiyuki Tomino, contributing to the production, and the character has remained a beloved pop cultural icon ever since.

However, Heidi, both the book and the anime, take place in the Swiss Alps. There’s no connection between the story and Yamanashi, and the placement of the park seems to be a result of Yamanashi being a fairly mountainous prefecture.

Similarly, the lunch buffet that Asami and her fellow travelers were here for wasn’t necessarily an edible snapshot of traditional Swiss cuisine. There was pot-au-feu, which is actually French in origin…

…and the fluffy rice omelet and karaage fried chicken are mainstays of modern Japanese cooking.

With the dishes themselves not being particularly exotic or unique, Asami, who generally hasn’t had good experiences in terms of buffet quality, mentally came to the preliminary conclusion that this wasn’t going to be a very tasty meal. After taking her first actual bite, though, she promptly ate her words, as everything turned out to be incredibly delicious, with her favorite of the bunch being the juicy, flavorful karaage (which, again, has no connection to Heidi).

Lunch finished at 2 o’clock, after which the group was free to explore the area at their own pace. Asami took a little time to look at some of the Heidi exhibits.

But before long she walked on over to…

…Heidi Village’s gigantic sunflower field!

With a semicircle of clouds shading part of the landscape but still a large enough patch of blue sky for sunlight to come streaming down from, Asami was able to get some great photos with the flowers’ colors really popping.

At 3 p.m., it was time to board the bus for the ride back to Tokyo, and at 5:50, Asami was back in Shinjuku.

All in all, it had been an unusual string of things not being exactly what Asami had expected. That doesn’t mean that she was overall disappointed, just that, despite her impression of bus tours as being a very predictable way of sightseeing, there turned out to be a lot of surprises, and the eclectic mix of experiences turned out to be a very enjoyable way to spend the day.

It wasn’t bad pricewise, either. Exact prices vary by date, but Asami’s tour cost her 8,290 yen (US$52). Considering that that included all of her transportation costs, the lunch buffet, the fruit brunch, and the Shingen Mochi desserts to take home, it felt like a good deal to her, and Asami thinks there are probably going to be more bus tours in her future.

title: Hot pot in cans coming to Japanese vending machines this fall
description: Or should we call them hot can? With September here, it won’t be long until Japan’s vending machines start getting stocked with hot beverages. On a crisp autumn afternoon or chilly winter night, there’s a special kind of comforting relaxation that comes from warming yourself up with some green tea or coffee, but this year […]
content:
Or should we call them hot can?

With September here, it won’t be long until Japan’s vending machines start getting stocked with hot beverages. On a crisp autumn afternoon or chilly winter night, there’s a special kind of comforting relaxation that comes from warming yourself up with some green tea or coffee, but this year you’ll also be able to get hot pot from Japan’s vending machines.

I suppose you could make the argument that, linguistically, these should be called hot can instead of hot pot, based on the containers they come in. That said, inside those cans is broth from the nabe (Japanese hot pot) base brand Shimenabe, produced by food company Mizkan. Shimenabe is one of Japan’s most popular brands of hot pot stock for home chefs, and now, thanks to a partnership with beverage company Dydo, two types are going to be sold as ready-to-drink canned hot pot soups.

The first, pictured above, is the Goma Tonyu, or Sesame Soy Milk, canned hot pot. Made with a chicken and vegetable stock, Dydo and Mizkan promise a rich, deep taste and enticing aroma. The second flavor is the Hotate and Hamaguri (Scallops and Clam) seafood hot pot, with a fish-based dashi stock and shellfish extract for a robust, complex flavor.

Both of the canned Shimenabe soups are done in a zosui style, meaning they have rice in them too, making them drinkable snacks for when you’re feeling both a little chilly and a little hungry. While the preview photos show their contents poured into a bowl and served with a spoon for a classy presentation, like all vending machine drinks these are actually meant to be sipped straight from the can.

Both versions of Dydo’s canned hot pot are priced at 160 yen (US$1) and will be appearing in vending machines, and in stores as well, starting October 26.

title: Does washing rice in this Japanese pouch really make it more delicious?
description: We test the Okome Pouch, which uses a patented method to make rice more delicious… and easier to wash. As much as we love rice, one thing we don’t particularly love is the work that goes into preparing it. Not only do you have to wash and knead the grains, but you often find yourself […]
content:
We test the Okome Pouch, which uses a patented method to make rice more delicious… and easier to wash.

As much as we love rice, one thing we don’t particularly love is the work that goes into preparing it. Not only do you have to wash and knead the grains, but you often find yourself scrambling to pick up errant grains when rinsing, before they disappear down the drain.

So when we heard about a product that claimed to “reproduce the ideal way of washing rice using patented technology, bringing out the full potential of each individual grain”, we knew we had to give it a try.

Called the Okome Pouch, with okome being the Japanese word for uncooked rice, the product is made in Japan from a gauze-like material, and comes with a drawstring opening.

The pouch comes in three sizes: 1-3 go, 1-6 go and 1-9 go, with “go” being the traditional Japanese unit used for measuring rice, which works out to be about 180 millilitres (about 0.76 U.S. cups).

We chose the 1-6 go variety, and after following the instructions to boil it before the very first use to sterilise it, we popped it into our rice-washing bowl and added the rice and water.

Pulling the opening closed, we then rinsed the rice by dunking the pouch up and down, before draining the water. Then we fully closed it by wrapping the rope around the opening, and kneaded the pouch for 15 to 30 seconds.

We tried “underwater kneading”, which involves kneading the pouch while it’s submerged in water, but apparently you can also do “air kneading”, where you knead without submersion or “rolling kneading”, where you roll it across a chopping board.

The underwater kneading turned the rice-washing water totally white, but after changing the water and rinsing it another two times, the prep was done, and best of all, no grains of rice had been spilled in the process.

While we usually leave the rice to soak in a bowl for around 30 minutes at this stage, when using this method you leave it to soak inside the pouch, for the same amount of time.

Then all that’s left to do is cook it the way you always do, which for us is in a donabe clay pot.

As soon as the cooking was done, we were very keen to test the results, starting first by judging their appearance.

▼ Regular bowl of rice on the left and the Okome Pouch version on the right.

At first glance, we didn’t notice much of a difference in appearance – perhaps the Okome Pouch version was a tad glossier. However, as soon as we tried a mouthful, we could tell it was clearly different from the rice we regularly make.

▼ The texture of the Okome Pouch-washed rice was noticeably softer, and each individual grain was wonderfully plump, without being soggy.

It wasn’t just us who noticed the difference, because when other members of the family, who knew nothing about the experiment, tasted the rice, they asked, “Is today’s rice different from usual?”

Though it’s hard to convey the difference through photos, it’s very noticeable in the eating. It was so noticeable that we took a closer look at the product description, where we learned that the secret apparently lies in the way the pouch forces most of the rice grains to come into contact with each other. When combined with the kneading motion, countless tiny scratches are created on the surface of the rice in a short amount of time. This allows the heat to penetrate the heart of each grain more effectively, producing plump, glossy rice.

After using the pouch, we were totally sold on it. Not only did it give us an easy and better way to wash the rice, it prevented the rice from spilling, and because it’s all contained within the pouch, it’s a handy way to prepare rice in less-than ideal environments, like while camping outdoors, or when you’ve just gotten your nails done.

You do have to wash the pouch after every use, but it only needs a quick wash, and it’s also dishwasher-safe, so it isn’t that much trouble. Priced at 1,920 yen (US$13), it can be purchased at homeware stores and online marketplace sites like Amazon and Rakuten, so keep an eye out for it if you want to upgrade your rice skills in the kitchen.

title: Can hanging a handy fan on your crotch keep you cool in the Tokyo summer? SN24 investigates
description: Mr. Sato and his crew strut through Shinjuku like cocks of the walk, but can their meat beat the heat? So…our plans to beat the summer heat haven’t exactly been going very well. Sure, the results have been moderately effective, but slapping 68 adhesive cooling patches on the upper body of our crack reporter Mr. […]
content:
Mr. Sato and his crew strut through Shinjuku like cocks of the walk, but can their meat beat the heat?

So…our plans to beat the summer heat haven’t exactly been going very well. Sure, the results have been moderately effective, but slapping 68 adhesive cooling patches on the upper body of our crack reporter Mr. Sato was also a pretty expensive endeavor. Likewise, yes, freezing our boss Yoshio’s hat in a block of ice did cool him off, but also took us more than a day and required an electric cutter and hand file to make wearable, making the process both time and labor-intensive.

And so it was that, once again, Mr. Sato sat at his desk in SoraNews24 headquarters, racking his brain for another countermeasure to the hot, humid weather.

Suddenly, inspiration struck, bringing with it a flash of glee to Mr. Sato’s face.

He rose to his feet, and his steps grew quicker and more excited with each step as he headed towards the door.

Honestly, at this point, we’ve stopped asking him questions when he does this sort of thing. All you can do is sit back and wait for the Sato surprise.

30 minutes later, Mr. Sato came bounding back into the office, holding…

…handy fans!

▼ “Hey guys! Look what I’ve got!”

Handy fans have become a trendy item in Tokyo these days. Advancements in mobile battery technology have brought them to a point where they’re affordable, relatively lightweight, and can run for a long time on a charge. Granted, they’re now commonplace enough to seem a little light on outside-the-box impact for one of Mr. Sato’s schemes, but Yoshio and fellow writer Seiji Nakazawa, who also happened to be in the office this day, were thankful all the same for Mr. Sato’s gifts.

Mr. Sato: “Here ya go, handy fans! The air conditioner alone doesn’t cut it on days as hot as this, right?”
Seiji: “Wow, thank you!”
Yoshio: “Thanks.”

Seiji: “Ahhh…so nice and cool!”
Yoshio: “It doesn’t get any better than this.”

But while smiles spread across Seiji and Yoshio’s faces, the one on Mr. Sato’s quickly vanished.

Mr. Sato: “Whoa, hold up! You’re just using them like normal? Did you dudes go brain-dead?”
Seiji: “Wha-?”
Yoshio: “Yes, what?”

Snatching their handy fans back, Mr. Sato fly into a rage and launched into a tirade.

Mr. Sato: “How many years have you ditzes been working at SoraNews24? ‘Ohhh, this feels so nice on my face’? That’s bush-league! That aint how we do things around here, and you know it!”

Mr. Sato: “I’ll show you both what to do! Geez, you’re not even worth wasting too punches on…here’s one for the both of ya!”
Seiji: “Gyahh!”
Yoshio: “So efficiently degrading!”

Mr. Sato: “Here, like this! If you’re a man, shut your mouth and hang the handy fan on your crotch!”

Mr. Sato: “Check it out! It makes you look awesome, like a Kamen Rider superhero belt!”

▼ ZUGYUUN (ズギューン), the sound of boldly showing off your crotch fan (see, Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure, you’re not the only one who can make up crazy sound effects).

▼ ZUGYUUN!

Mr. Sato: “OK, now you two guys do it!”
Seiji: “Like this?”
Yoshio: “Is this correct?”

Mr. Sato: “Yeah, that’s more like it.”
Seiji: “You know, this really is cooler.”
Yoshio: “You could almost say it’s cold.”
Mr. Sato: “See? I told you guys.”

Mr. Sato: “OK, time to move out.”
Seiji: “We’re going outside dressed like weirdos again?”
Yoshio: “I’m not so sure about this.”

Mr. Sato: “Not so sure? Come on man, you’ve gone outside wearing stranger stuff than this. You know what’s going to get us in trouble, and it’s not this.”
Seiji: “Well, I guess he’s right…”

Yoshio: “So where are we going?”
Mr. Sato: “Yoshio, baby, you don’t need to ask that. You know exactly where we’re going.”
Yoshio: “Well, yeah, but if I have to ask to establish context for our readers, don’t I?”
Mr. Sato: “Well, how very proper and responsible of you.”

Seiji: “How many times does this make that we’ve gone ‘there’ doing stuff like this?”
Mr. Sato: “I can’t even remember. Doesn’t change anything though. Gotta be done.”
Yoshio: “At this point, it feels like some mysterious sense of obligation.”

Mr. Sato: “OK, stay sharp until we get across the street.”
Yoshio: “Why?”

Mr. Sato: “Dude, because we’re passing in front of the police box.”
Seiji: “Hey, weren’t you the one saying we weren’t going to get in any trouble?”
Mr. Sato: “Hey, just being extra cautious.”

Mr. Sato: “Once we get across, we’ll be out of the danger zone.”
Yoshio: “Focus…focus…”

Mr. Sato: “See, we made it. Back again at our good old local Starbucks.”
Seiji: “Seems like we always find our way back here at times like this.”
Mr. Sato: “Is there anyplace better?”
Yoshio: “I’ve got to admit, you’re right about that.”

Mr. Sato: “Aaaand coffee cheers!”
Seiji: “The coffee here always feels like it comes with a sense of accomplishment on the side.”
Yoshio: “Somehow, making it here always feels like we just crossed a finish line.”

title: 7-Eleven Japan’s Ramen Machine is a viral hit, but there’s one glaring problem
description: Well, two if you take into account how rare they are to find.  7-Eleven has been forging ahead of the convenience store pack in recent years with its range of automated countertop machines, letting customers whip up their own freshly made coffee, tea and smoothies. While the chain’s drink machines are widely known, not many […]
content:
Well, two if you take into account how rare they are to find. 

7-Eleven has been forging ahead of the convenience store pack in recent years with its range of automated countertop machines, letting customers whip up their own freshly made coffee, tea and smoothies.

While the chain’s drink machines are widely known, not many people know that at some branches you can find special ramen machines, which use the same system of automation to turn frozen ramen into piping hot, ready-to-eat ramen, all in a matter of seconds.

Despite having gone viral when they were first introduced, with the chain’s original introductory video receiving over 7 million views, the machines remain a hidden gem, as they can only be found at 40 locations, all in Tokyo’s neighbouring Saitama Prefecture.

After trying the machines in December last year and again in May, we’ve been waiting for them to be rolled out at more locations, but alas, the number of stores offering them has remained unchanged, sitting at 40, all in Saitama.

▼ The ramen varieties have expanded, though, with Taiwanese Mazesoba and Beef Udon recently added to the range.

When our reporter P.K. Sanjun headed out to Saitama to try the noodles, he came across an inherent problem which he’d like to share, as he thinks it might be one of the reasons why the machines haven’t been installed nationwide.

▼ First, though, he picked out a tub of noodles from the freezer and paid for it at the counter.

Popping the noodles into the machine, he was happy to find that it was an intuitive process, as he just needed to press a button and wait for the machine to do its thing.

As he watched, he was instantly impressed by the speed of it all, because less than a minute after putting the frozen ramen into the machine, and watching the giant metal rod pierce through the plastic lid to whip it up…

▼ … a piping-hot bowl of ramen was ready.

Normally, frozen ramen takes around three minutes in a microwave, or about five minutes if heating it up on a stovetop. The fact that the ramen takes just around a minute to be ready is a big part of the machine’s appeal, but after he took it out of the machine, that’s when he realised the one glaring problem with it.

▼ “Where am I supposed to eat this ramen?”

Like most 7-Elevens, this one didn’t have an eat-in space, and one of the staff members sensed his unease, saying, “Sorry, we don’t have anywhere for you to sit! I guess everyone eats theirs in their cars?”

Well, if he’d driven here, in-car eating would definitely be a good option, but he’d come here by public transport, and to make matters worse, it was raining that day. With one hand occupied with the task of holding an umbrella and the other holding a bowl of seriously piping-hot ramen, the whole experience almost felt like some sort of punishment.

When he did get around to tasting it, he found himself feeling incredibly self-conscious as he had to slurp up his noodles while standing outside the store, in front of arriving cars and curious passersby.

▼ P.K.’s alfresco dining setting.

Despite the embarrassment, the ramen itself turned out to be very tasty – the noodles had a satisfyingly firm texture, and the broth was hot and flavourful. At around 700 yen (US$4.38), it wasn’t a bad deal, especially considering the fact that it takes a minute to make and is available 24 hours a day.

Still, at stores in major cities and busy downtown areas in particular, you’re likely to run into the “Where am I supposed to eat this ramen?” problem. So in that sense, perhaps the ramen machine is better suited to regional areas, where people are more likely to be travelling by car.

In any case, 7-Eleven’s ramen machines are still going strong in Saitama so there’s no signs of them disappearing yet. Here’s hoping they make their way into Tokyo soon, so city workers like P.K. can enjoy them in the office, rather than having to eat them outside on the street.

title: Burger King goes viral in Japan for opening new store in a Japanese-style building
description: U.S. dining and Japanese architectural design come together at this eye-catching new location. Burger King has carved out a unique niche for itself in Japan, doing things differently to its competitors with all-you-can-eat deals, unusual menu items, and a vibe that’s arguably more independent and adventurous. That sense of bold free-spiritedness is currently on display […]
content:
U.S. dining and Japanese architectural design come together at this eye-catching new location.

Burger King has carved out a unique niche for itself in Japan, doing things differently to its competitors with all-you-can-eat deals, unusual menu items, and a vibe that’s arguably more independent and adventurous.

That sense of bold free-spiritedness is currently on display at a recently opened store in Noda City, Chiba Prefecture. Described as unconventional, the new branch has been attracting a considerable amount of attention online due to the building it’s housed in, as it looks like a traditional Japanese building.

The first thing you’ll notice about this branch is the roof, which is tiled in a way that makes it look like a traditional Japanese house. Seeing the Burger King sign on a roof like this looks totally out of the norm, creating a unique blend of Japanese tradition and fast-food Americana not commonly seen in Japan.

To a local, this is a very odd combination, because on the rare occasion that you see a big-name chain set up home in a traditional building in Japan, like this Starbucks in Kyoto, the signage and branding is also subdued to match the old-fashioned landscape.

▼ There’s no dialling down the Burger King branding here, as the sign stands loud and proud on the roof, just as it would on a regular-looking storefront.

Stepping closer reveals even more unique details, with a beautiful metallic rain chain by the front doors.

These rain chains are usually only seen on traditional homes or shrine and temple buildings.

Stepping through the front doors, however, reveals a very modern interior that makes it clear you’re in a Burger King.

As it turns out, this building used to be home to Aozora, a tempura restaurant by sushi conveyor belt restaurant chain Sushiro. When the new Burger King took over, it redid the interior and kept the Japanese-style facade, creating a unique branch.

▼ Wood and brick panelling gives the inside a very Western look.

Despite being newly opened, this was already a popular branch, with a constant flow of people coming and going through the doors when we visited. While some were clearly interested in the facade, stopping to take photos as they made their way from their cars, others were more interested in the food, especially with steak specials on the menu.

We couldn’t stop by a Burger King without trying something, so we bypassed the steak and opted for something a little more in line with the traditional vibe of the building.

▼ A Teriyaki Whopper Set…plus a Whopper Cheese Jr. to keep the U.S. fusion blend going.

Burger King burgers are known for being hefty, so staff are happy to cut them in half if you request it.

▼ The Teriyaki Whopper was delicious, giving us the salty sweet flavours of Japan.

▼ While the Jr. gave us the meaty American burger taste we’d been craving.

▼ It was a delicious meal made even more delicious by the sweet fusion style of the building.

So next time you find yourself craving a side of Japan with your Burger King burger, this humble branch has you covered. It’s nice to see the chain keeping the beauty of a traditional Japanese-style building alive, and there are plenty of other beautiful restaurant buildings we’d be happy to see the chain take up residence in too.

description: Can we demolish a four-kilo purin made with 32 eggs?  Be careful what you wish for. content:
Can we demolish a four-kilo purin made with 32 eggs? 

Be careful what you wish for. That’s something we’ve often heard wise people say, but we’re not always wise, nor are we always good listeners. That’s what led us to a cafe in Tokyo’s upscale Omotesando district the other day, where we pulled up a chair and ordered the stuff of dreams: a four-kilo purin.

That’s 8.8 pounds if you’re going by the Imperial system, and if you’re wondering what purin is it’s Japanese pudding, made with custard and similar to a flan or creme caramel. It’s also our reporter Natsuki Gojo’s favourite dessert, so when she heard about the massive, big-eats version, she immediately raced out to try it.

It was only when she arrived at the cafe, called Sweet Check, when the reality of what she was about to do hit her, and although she’d invited a friend to join her, she was unsure about whether or not they would be able to finish the huge dessert.

Still, eating massive amounts of endless pudding had always been a dream of hers, so she was determined to give it her all. However, when staff brought over a tray that took up almost the entire table, with a huge mould on top of it, she began to feel her pulse quicken.

When the mould was gradually removed, her eyes widened as the dessert slowly revealed itself.

Then, when the mould was completely released, the caramel sauce came flooding out like a waterfall.

▼ She was now face-to-face with her dream giant pudding!!!

Staff told her that this sweet beast weighs around 4 kilos and is made using 32 eggs and two litres (68 ounces) of milk. Natsuki had never thought about what actually goes into her favourite dessert so she decided to block the mental image of eating two dozen eggs in one sitting, and dipped her spoon into the silky smooth pudding for a taste.

It was a beautifully firm pudding, and the first bite revealed the rich flavour of custard, just how she likes it.

The caramel sauce had quite a strong bitterness, which helped to balance out the sweetness, and it felt decadent to eat it directly from the tray with spoons.

▼ If you prefer a fancier presentation, it can also be cut into pieces for serving, but we recommend carving out chunks with your spoon.

Natsuki was thankful that it wasn’t overly sweet, so she could easily eat mouthful after delicious mouthful. As she continued eating, she noticed that things were particularly creamy and delicious near the base of the dessert, where there appeared to be a thin layer of something different.

After asking staff about it, they told her this layer formed naturally under the weight of the pudding, and although it happens with all purin, it was more noticeable here due to its massive size.

▼ You can see the layer here, in white.

Natsuki felt it was a privilege to taste this exquisite creaminess, seeing as it’s something you can’t really detect in a regular pudding, and it gave her extra encouragement to keep going. At this point, she began to feel confident that she and her friend might actually be able to eat nearly all of the pudding, but as they continued eating, they both gradually began to feel full.

In the end, they put down their spoons and admitted defeat, because after eating about a third of it, they were unable to go on. Realising that the bounds of her stomach couldn’t match the vast bounds of her love for purin, Natsuki began to feel slightly defeated at her efforts. However, staff told her not to worry, as they’d never even seen a group of four finish one – they said you’d probably need around six people to eat the whole thing.

Thankfully, the leftover pudding can be taken home, which came as a welcome relief to our purin-loving duo. They probably left more than three kilos behind, so the bags they left with were incredibly heavy.

▼ The purin can also be freezed, so Natsuki’s visit wasn’t in vain as she now gets to enjoy pudding at home for weeks to come.

If you’d like to test your own purin powers, you’ll need to make a reservation at least two days in advance, as the giant pudding takes six hours to bake and one day to chill and set. There’s also a limit on how many can be made each day, so you’ll want to make your reservation as soon as you’ve decided on the date you’d like to visit.

At 5,000 yen (US$32.55) it’s a very affordable deal, especially if you’re going with a group, and it’ll definitely be a dining experience to remember. Just be sure to come on an empty stomach, and be careful what you wish for!
